summary: Gives an implementation specification for the Data Reconfiguration Service proposed in RFC 138. The service converts data between the forms used by different computers on the network. The authors come from several institutions, including UCLA, Rand, MIT, SDC, UCSB and MITRE.

plainLanguage.summary: The Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS) changes a data stream from one format to another. A user can ask it to apply a stored set of rules, called a form, between a user process and a serving process.

subtitle: A design for storing named data transformations and applying them to network streams.

tldr.problem: Programs and terminals use different data formats, so data prepared for one may not suit another.
tldr.mechanism: The Data Reconfiguration Service stores named forms. Its Form Machine applies each form's ordered rules to an input stream and produces a reformatted output stream.
tldr.outcome: The authors describe the service as an experiment intended to explore principles for a possible future standard service.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 166 as Unknown, with no RFC listed as updating or obsoleting it. The text describes DRS as an experiment that might inform a future standard service.

sections.title: Why Reconfigure Data
sections.content:
Application programs often require different input and output formats. The authors propose adapting data to each program, rather than requiring every program to use one format. The same issue arises when different consoles connect to one service program.

A programmer defines a form describing a transformation, and the DRS stores it by name. Later, a user can call that form by name to transform a network data stream. The notation is designed to be useful for the experiment without becoming a general-purpose programming language.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs may expect the same information in different formats. A stored form lets the service change the data for a program without requiring the program to change its own format.

sections.title: Connections and Service Commands
sections.content:
A DRS implementation includes connection handling, request processing, a compiler or interpreter called the Form Machine, and storage for forms. Three conceptual connections are used: the control connection between the originating user and DRS, the user connection between a user process and DRS, and the server connection between DRS and the serving process.

The user defines, lists and purges forms over the control connection, and can request simplex or duplex connections that apply forms to data. The DRS acknowledges each command line. A form's termination or failure can be reported with a host, socket and return code. The user and serving processes need only an NCP interface, according to the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: One connection lets a user manage forms, while two other connections carry data between a user process and a server. The DRS applies the selected form as that data passes through.

sections.title: How the Form Machine Works
sections.content:
A form is an ordered set of rules. Each rule can describe data to match in the input stream and data to emit in the output stream. Terms can name data, describe its type and length, repeat it, compare values or assign values. If a rule succeeds, the input and output positions advance as described; if a match fails, processing normally continues with the next rule.

The listed data types are B (bit string), O (bit string), X (bit string), E (EBCDIC character) and A (Network ASCII character). Control options can transfer to another rule, and R terminates the form and returns a code. Arithmetic expressions are evaluated left to right with no precedence.
sections.plainLanguage: A form checks pieces of incoming data and describes what to write out. Its rules can also repeat fields, compare values, or choose another rule when a match succeeds or fails.

sections.title: Examples and Limits
sections.content:
The examples show forms that add line numbers, omit a field, convert variable-length EBCDIC records to ASCII, add a length field, reorder fields, and pack or unpack repeated characters. These examples illustrate how one form can carry out a specific data-reformatting task.

The RFC limits binary lengths to 32 bits, character strings to 256 characters, identifiers to 4 characters, the number of identifiers to 256, and rule labels to 0 through 9999.
sections.plainLanguage: The sample forms add, remove, convert, count or reorder data fields. The notation has explicit limits, including a maximum string length of 256 characters.

references.text: RFC 138, a proposal for the Data Reconfiguration Service.
